tip: Weather uses fare, not essere: fa freddo = it's cold, fa caldo = it's hot.
mano is feminine even though it ends in -o: la mano, and the plural is le mani.
gli is the masculine plural 'the' before a vowel or s+consonant: gli occhi, gli amici.
Io is optional; the -o ending of parlo already means I, so Italians usually drop it.
quanto agrees with its noun: quante persone (feminine plural), quanti giorni (masculine plural).
a + la merge into one word: alla porta = at the door.
Italian turns meals into verbs: pranzare = to have lunch, so tu pranzi = you have lunch.
bello shortens to bel before a masculine noun: bel tempo, un bel film.
si + essere says it broke on its own, and the participle agrees: si è rotto il telefono (masculine).
After piacere an infinitive stays singular: gli piace giocare, never piacciono giocare.
piacere agrees with the thing liked, not with you: i ragni is plural, so it becomes piacciono.
fare male = to hurt: mi fa male un dente means a tooth hurts me, with the body part as subject.
Nationality adjectives are lowercase and agree: cucina italiana, vino italiano.
qualcosa di + adjective stays masculine singular: qualcosa di strano = something strange.
Italian doubles the negative: non c'è nessuno needs both words to say there's nobody.
Adjectives ending in -e don't change for gender: facile is the same for masculine and feminine.
meno = less for comparisons; its opposite is più = more: meno rumorosa = less noisy.
An object pronoun attaches to the end of an infinitive: averlo = avere + lo = to have it.
Singular family members drop the article: mio nonno, mia madre, not il mio nonno.
Comparisons use più ... di: più grande della mia = bigger than mine, with di + la = della.
dare fastidio a = to bother someone: le dà fastidio = it bothers her.
The person who likes is marked with a: A Marco piace la chitarra = Marco likes the guitar.
Italian uses the article for times of day: la mattina = in the morning, la sera = in the evening.
